title: Association Between Social Media Screen Time and Depression and Anxiety Among Adolescents: A Systematic Review
venue: International Journal of Education Pedagogy and Psychology
abstract: Social media use by youth is nearly a universal phenomenon. Adolescents of this generation find it very challenging to envision a life without social media. Despite its pervasive use among children and adolescents, there has been very little research conducted to understand the impact of time spent on social media on children, especially on their mental health and wellbeing. This systematic review examines the extent to which social media screen time is associated between depressive and anxiety symptoms among adolescents aged 10-19 years. Following the PRISMA 2020 Statement, six databases and Google Scholar were searched, of which fifty eligibility studies were retrieved which was published between January 2015 and August 2026, comprising 33 cross-sectional and 17 cohort designs. Two independent reviewers partitioned records, extracted data, and assessed methodological quality using the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Critical Appraisal Checklists for cross-sectional and cohort studies. As a result of the substantial heterogeneity in exposure and outcome measures, a narrative synthesis of the findings was more relevant than statistical pooling. The majority of studies reported a significant positive association between social media use and depressive symptoms, with the recent cohort studies using within-person analytic techniques strengthening this association. Evidence for anxiety was directionally similar but weaker, less consistent, and in several studies non-linear. The key moderating and mediating factors were gender, sleep disruptions, cyberbullying, active vs. passive engagement, and familial and peer environments. Quality appraisal indicated a generally sound evidence base, with all cross-sectional studies rated high quality, confidence was limited by widespread dependence on unvalidated self-report exposure measures and unclear baseline symptom status in the cohort studies. These findings support a shift in clinical practice, policy, and future research away from screen-time limits alone and toward assessing the pattern, content, and context of adolescent social media use. Keywords: mental health; Depression; Anxiety; Adolescents; social media screen time

claims.text: Approximately four in five reviewed studies reported a statistically significant positive association between social media screen time or problematic use and depressive symptoms.

Cohort studies using within-person analytic techniques found that within-person increases in social media use predicted subsequent increases in depressive symptoms after accounting for baseline levels.
Evidence linking social media screen time to anxiety was weaker and less consistent across studies compared to evidence linking it to depression.
Two large cohort studies observed a non-linear, U-shaped relationship where moderate social media use was associated with lower anxiety symptoms than persistently low or high use.
The association between social media use and depressive symptoms was generally stronger among female adolescents than male adolescents.
Sleep disruption and cyberbullying were identified as key mediating pathways linking adolescent social media use with mental health distress.
Passive social media use was more strongly associated with internalizing symptoms than active social media use.
Problematic or compulsive social media use scales were more strongly and consistently associated with distress than raw screen-time duration measures.
All 33 cross-sectional studies were rated high quality under JBI appraisal, whereas 10 of 17 cohort studies were rated high quality and 7 were rated moderate quality.
The validity and reliability of the social media exposure measure was rated unclear in 79% of cross-sectional studies and 82% of cohort studies.
Eighty-eight percent of included cohort studies did not establish that participants were free of depressive or anxiety outcomes at baseline.

limitations.text: Substantial heterogeneity in social media exposure definitions and over fifteen different depression and anxiety outcome instruments precluded meta-analysis, requiring a less quantitatively precise narrative synthesis.

The literature search was restricted to English-language peer-reviewed publications, which may have excluded relevant evidence in other languages or in grey literature and introduced potential publication bias.
The review restricted eligibility to cross-sectional and cohort designs, excluding qualitative and experimental evidence.
The retrieved evidence base was predominantly concentrated in high-income, Western countries, limiting global generalizability to low- and middle-income regions.
Included primary studies relied heavily on unvalidated, self-report single-item exposure measures prone to recall and reporting bias.
Most included cohort studies failed to confirm that participants were symptom-free at baseline, impeding clear causal inference and temporal ordering.

future_work.text: Develop and use social media exposure measures with established validity and reliability, ideally supplemented by device-recorded objective screen-time data.
Conduct longitudinal cohort studies that explicitly establish baseline freedom from depressive and anxiety symptoms and transparently explore loss to follow-up.
Implement experimental and intervention designs capable of establishing causal directions rather than relying solely on observational associations.
Explicitly test and model non-linear dose-response relationships between social media use and mental health outcomes, especially for anxiety.
Expand empirical research into adolescent populations in low- and middle-income countries across Africa, South America, and South Asia.
Conduct subgroup meta-analyses using standardized instruments like PHQ-9 and GAD-7 paired with standardized daily hours measures.
